blocks.heading: A store manager asks: which product categories generate the most revenue?

items.question: Her options today
items.text: Wait about **three days** for an analyst, learn the schema and SQL herself, or wait weeks for a curated tool.
items.action: Published scores fall from **91.2 %** on Spider 1.0 to **21.3 %** on enterprise tasks: a good demo is not evidence.

items.question: What she needs
items.text: An answer **today**, the **SQL behind it** so she can check it, and her data **never changed**.
items.action: Other tools pay for meaning in setup; this project pays in **review**.

items.question: Why it is hard
items.text: Words like “revenue” are not columns; real schemas can exceed **1,000** columns.
items.action: And generated SQL runs on real data, so it must never change it.

items.question: Who else it serves
items.text: Managers new to a database, privacy-sensitive teams and teams with large schemas.
items.action: Not for metrics that must match across teams.

blocks.heading: One question’s path: one model call, two gates in code, then back to her
blocks.alt: Flowchart of the app in four stage lanes: prepare, generate, check and run, answer.
blocks.caption: Stages left to right, steps top to bottom. Yellow is the model, teal is enforced in code.

items.heading: Her answer
items.label: Electronics; the SQL shows it counts **all 220 orders**.

blocks.heading: Local 9B model: 64.6 % on Spider, 35.2 % on BIRD
blocks.caption: Answers matching the reference rows; this project’s scorer, not leaderboard scoring.

blocks.heading: On large databases, fewer tables scored higher
blocks.caption: 1,222 questions: **+3.6 [+1.4, +5.8]**, about 2 s slower. A dropped table cut top 6 to **5.4 %**; five later trials added no accuracy.

blocks.heading: Four tests would close the main gaps before any default changes

items.question: New large schemas
items.text: The gain is from **2 of 4** databases.

blocks.text: **A first, checkable answer** for people who know the question but not the schema.
